local_facts.title: Half the value, and the whole house is new construction
local_facts.claim: The City of Biloxi's 2023 floodplain guidance says that if improvements, additions or repairs to an existing structure in the flood zone cost at least half of its market value, materials and labor counted, the city and the National Flood Insurance Program require the entire structure to meet new-construction requirements, including elevation to one foot above the base flood elevation. Nearly half of the land in Biloxi is in a special flood hazard area, nearly all of Point Cadet is in a flood zone, and dumping into ditches and streams violates city ordinance Sec. 9-1-15.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A remodel that crosses the half-value line turns into an elevation job, and the debris multiplies with it. Containers also have to stay out of the ditch line, which in a city this low carries the street's runoff.

local_facts.title: Curbside service stops at contractor debris
local_facts.claim: Biloxi's trash guide says garbage, recycling and yard trash are collected under a contract through the Harrison County Utility Authority, and that contractor-generated waste such as construction debris, or limbs left by tree or lawn services, will not be picked up because removal is the contractor's responsibility. Concrete, asphalt, dirt and tires are also on the not-collected list, and nothing placed in the right-of-way in front of an empty lot is picked up. A 2016 city notice directed contractor debris to the rubbish landfill on Hudson-Krohn Road.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Any renovation, roof or demolition in Biloxi needs its own container and a permitted place to dump it. Debris piled at the curb gets left there.

local_facts.title: Two classes of rubbish site decide where a load can go
local_facts.claim: Mississippi rules let a Class I rubbish site accept construction and demolition debris, brick, concrete, cardboard, vegetation, furniture and similar waste, while a Class II site accepts only natural vegetation and inert material such as brick, mortar, concrete, stone and asphalt. Household garbage, liquids, paint and chemical containers, whole tires, batteries, refrigerators and air conditioners are barred from both. MDEQ's active facility listing shows a Class I rubbish landfill and a transfer station at 14339 Hudson Krohn Road in Biloxi, further Class I sites near Pass Christian and Saucier, a Class II site on Road 510 in Biloxi, and the county's municipal solid waste landfill at Pecan Grove near Pass Christian.
local_facts.why_it_matters: What is in the container decides where it can be dumped. A clean load of concrete or brick qualifies for the simplest sites, mixed renovation debris needs a Class I site, and household garbage needs a landfill rather than a rubbish site.

local_facts.title: Katrina left Biloxi nearly three million cubic yards
local_facts.claim: By July 22, 2007, the City of Biloxi had hauled more than 2.94 million cubic yards of Hurricane Katrina debris and estimated more than 98 percent of it removed, with debris removal and disposal projected to cost $79.7 million. At the six-month mark, unburnable debris made up 1,625,112 of the 2,078,194 cubic yards hauled from city streets and rights-of-way. By August 2007 the city had issued more than 3,984 building permits for storm repairs.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Public debris contracts clear streets and rights-of-way. What comes out of a damaged house, from sheetrock to slab, is the owner's or the contractor's to remove, and on this coast that work arrives in waves after every storm.

anchors.label: FORTIFIED roof grant for wind-pool policyholders
anchors.detail: From July 1, 2026 the Mississippi Insurance Department funds roofs built to the FORTIFIED Roof standard for homeowners insured three consecutive years with the Mississippi Windstorm Underwriting Association. A statewide rollout is expected in early 2027. Every grant roof starts as a tear-off.
